newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: China balks at U.N. peacekeepers in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: China balks at U.N. peacekeepers in Guatemala.

text.p: China on Thursday balked at sending military observers to Guatemala to implement its new peace agreement aimed at ending more than three decades of civil war, diplomats said.

Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in reports to the Security Council, said 155 military officers and some medical personnel were needed for three months to verify the peace settlement, due for signature on Dec. 29.

But envoys said Beijing told council members that Guatemala's actions threatened China's "territorial integrity," an apparent reference to the Central American country's support of moves aimed at securing membership for Taiwan in the United Nations. China replaced Taiwan in the world body in 1971.

China did not threaten to veto the peacekeepers but diplomats feared Beijing might do so. They said a veto would jeopardise implementation of the agreement, which includes an intricate timetable for the separation of forces, disarmament and demobilization.

A similar pattern emerged each time peacekeepers for Haiti were due for approval and China threatened to veto the contingents, mainly because of Haiti's relations with Taiwan. Approval was eventually given for a reduced number of troops.
Peace talks between the government and the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) began more than five years ago, but progress was slow until the United Nations began mediating in 1994.

More than 100,000 people have died in Guatemala's 36-year armed conflict, and a further 40,000 have "disappeared," with the army accused of human rights abuses against the country's indigenous people.
Boutros-Ghali said the military component of the agreements should be on the ground within two weeks of the accords being signed to investigate any violations.
Under these provisions, Guatemala's army will redeploy units to specified locations, and URNG troops will move to eight assembly points.

Unarmed U.N. military observers are to verify a ceasefire and patrol a security zone around each assembly point. The guerrillas eventually are to hand over their weapons and uniforms to Guatemalan and U.N. personnel before leaving the assembly points.
Boutros-Ghali suggested that the council grant him "contingent authority" to move military observers into place as soon as possible after the agreement is signed.
"Authorization for the actual deployment of the component would be sought as soon as it is confirmed that the final peace agreement has been signed," he said in his report.
